summary:
Daegu stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The armed forces are the exception: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether. Legal gender recognition is available, and on 8 May 2024 a court ruled that requiring sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status violates physical integrity.

Daegu hosts the country's second-largest LGBT event, a pride parade and film programme running a week or two, usually in late June. The Daegu Queer Culture Festival has been held every year since June 2009 without interruption, most recently on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro.

Organised opposition is annual and recurrent, and it is contained by the courts rather than by the state declining to act. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee sought injunctions against the festival in 2022, 2023, 2024 and again in 2025; the Daegu District Court dismissed each bid. An estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups form a standing countermeasure committee in Daegu to block LGBT events, and that opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central street.

Police practice constrains the march itself. Officers again restricted the 2025 route to a single bus-only lane, and the Daegu District Court has found the police notice restricting the event legitimate on the ground that Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. In 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. Organisers framed the 2025 event as resistance to hate and discriminatory politics.

Mobilisation against the festival is large and well organised. A Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer' response in September 2025, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450-metre stretch toward the Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans.

Venue restriction remained live into the 2026 edition. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters, comprising the Daegu-Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea demanding a change of festival venue on public-welfare grounds, claiming about 34,000 signatures and describing that as unusually large for a single Commission petition. The petition answers a January filing by the festival committee against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act.
tangentialFactors:
Daegu's pattern of contained but persistent opposition sits within a national climate in which anti-LGBT mobilisation has at times turned violent. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors while accusing police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. No comparable violence at the Daegu festival is documented in the sources.

National attitude data give context to the local mobilisation: Pew Research Center found 18% of South Koreans felt homosexuality should be tolerated in 2007, rising to 39% in 2013. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

Trans-specific harms documented nationally are not tied to Daegu in these sources: restroom avoidance in schools and public buildings, a National Human Rights Commission finding of a transgender hospitalisation blind spot in November 2023, and the compulsory discharge and posthumous reinstatement of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su. Visitors should expect these as national conditions rather than Daegu-specific ones.
localsOnly:
The opposition structure in Daegu is institutional and locally rooted. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters brings together a parents' alliance, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, meaning the merchants' association of the very street the festival uses is a party to the demand for relocation.

The annual countermeasure mobilisation has a fixed calendar of its own, now in its seventeenth year, drawing congregations from across the Daegu and Gyeongbuk area to a set route through the city centre.

Local LGBT organisers have pursued their own legal route: the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker targets Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act, the provision under which police route notices for the march are issued.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the June 2026 petition to the National Human Rights Commission of Korea is unresolved in the sources; whether the Commission acted on the venue demand, and whether any further court challenge to the 2026 route followed, is not sourced here.

No Daegu-specific record of physical violence against trans people, hate-crime reporting, or police handling of anti-trans incidents in the city is present in the inventory. The violence figures cited are national or from other cities.

The claim that the festival is the country's second-largest LGBT event rests on secondary reference material rather than an attendance dataset, and the Pew tolerance figures date from 2007 and 2013 and do not measure attitudes in Daegu specifically.

Whether the 2023 municipal road-blocking by city officials resulted in any judicial finding is not stated in the sources.
